question: Which feature of cancer biology makes population-level screening programmes for solid tumours feasible?

answers.text: Most carcinomas metastasise immediately after the first malignant transformation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. If metastasis occurred immediately, early detection would offer no survival benefit.

answers.text: Most carcinomas evolve slowly through a recognisable pre-invasive stage before becoming locally invasive

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The long pre-invasive phase (e.g., CIN in cervical cancer, adenoma in colorectal cancer) creates a detection window during which intervention can prevent progression.

answers.text: All carcinomas express specific serum biomarkers from the time of first cellular transformation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Most early cancers do not produce detectable serum markers; it is the biological pre-invasive progression that creates the screening window.

answers.text: Carcinoma-in-situ lesions are always visible on standard imaging

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Many pre-invasive lesions require specific screening modalities (e.g., cytology, colonoscopy) and are not visible on standard imaging.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the biology of cancer progression. The key concept is the pre-invasive phase — for most solid cancers this phase is long enough to permit organised screening to detect lesions before invasion.
Excellent. The slow progression through a pre-invasive stage is the biological basis for effective screening — it creates the window in which detection and intervention can alter outcome.
